title: GPU suspend-resume deadlock triage playbook (draft)
body:
Purpose and scope:
This is a working draft playbook for oncall SREs and GPU lab engineers to triage a specific class of instability weve been seeing: reproducible driver hangs and kernel panics that occur after suspend/resume (host power-state transitions, maintenance window PM cycles, or rack-level power-cycling), often manifesting as: ECC bursts followed by blocked DMA, nvidia driver deadlock, or kernel OOPS tied to the GPU PCIe device.

Why this is different from general ECC/NVLink notes:
- Events cluster after PM events (suspend to RAM, S3-like cycles, or BIOS-induced power gating) rather than steady-state thermal/ECC drift.
- Reproduces well in lab when host power-state transitions are exercised.
- Symptoms include: device disappears from nvidia-smi, subsequent driver unload fails, and heavy dmesg error sequences mentioning "GPU hang: DRM lockup" or "DMA engine stuck".

Quick oncall checklist (first 15 minutes):
1) If incident is active and customer impact is severe: trigger mitigations (rolling reboot of affected rack) and page oncall infra lead.
2) Collect immediate artifacts: dmesg -T (last 2000 lines), journalctl -k --no-pager --since "-30m", nvidia-smi -q -d MEMORY, lspci -vvv -s <gpu-pci>, lsmod | grep nvidia, /var/log/syslog or cloud-agent logs.
3) Snapshot kernel oops: save /proc/interrupts and /proc/driver/nvidia/version when possible.
4) If node is unresponsive to SSH but still on network, ask fab or colo to perform controlled soft power-cycle; avoid hard AC cycles unless required.
5) Mark affected hosts in incident doc and add tag "suspend-resume-class".

Commands we commonly run (copy/paste friendly):
- dmesg -T | tail -n 500 > /tmp/dmesg-incident.log
- journalctl -b -1 --no-pager > /tmp/journal-previous-boot.log  # if suspect resume from last boot
- nvidia-smi -q -d ALL > /tmp/nvidia-smi-all.log || true
- uname -a > /tmp/uname.log; cat /proc/driver/nvidia/version > /tmp/nvidia-version || true
- ls -la /var/crash || true  # kernel crash dumps might be present

Quick mitigations (short-term):
- Prefer a graceful reboot of the host instead of letting it keep in hung state to avoid repeated hangs.
- If location permits, disable host suspend/resume in BIOS and OS power management (workaround: set /etc/systemd/sleep.conf to AllowSuspend=no).
- Add temporary auto-fallback: route workload away from nodes that have seen a PM transition in past 4 hours (via fleet metadata label), until root cause known.

Lab repro recipe (lab SRE / applied-ML steps):
Goal: produce a reliable reproduce in small lab rack with same kernel + driver stack.
1) Start from the exact AMI/container image used in production (note kernel and nvidia driver versions).
2) Run a continuous GPU load: python -c "from time import sleep; import torch; x=torch.randn(2048,2048,device='cuda'); [x.matmul(x) for _ in range(1000)]; sleep(3600)" or run existing stress harness.
3) Trigger suspend/resume: echo mem > /sys/power/state OR use systemctl suspend; wait for resume. For BIOS-level AC cycles, simulate with controlled IPMI soft power-cycle.
4) After resume, continuously poll dmesg and nvidia-smi for first 30 minutes.
5) Capture kernel trace if hang appears: echo 1 > /proc/sys/kernel/sysrq; echo c > /proc/sysrq-trigger to create crash dump (lab only).
6) Experiment variations: enable/disable ASPM in kernel boot args, toggle IOMMU on/off, test with different PCIe link speeds and cable lengths (for NVLink-connected multi-GPU nodes).

Target signals and log patterns (what to look for):
- Repeated lines with "NVRM: Xid (PCI): 79, 31" or new Xid codes after resume.
- "GPU Hang detected" followed by "GPU reset failed"
- Driver messages: "failed to get dma-buf", "DMA engine timeout" or stack traces referencing nvkm/preserve functions.
- PCI link retrain messages in kernel logs.
- Any kernel softlockup or watchdog timeout right after resume.

Hypotheses (ranked, with short rationale):
1) Driver state not fully reinitialized after PM paths: driver keeps stale DMA descriptors after host resumes -> DMA engine lock. (High plausibility; multiple lab reproductions.)
2) Firmware/PM handshake bug: GPU microcode doesn't complete PM quiesce/resume sequence -> HW queues left in inconsistent state. (Medium plausibility; vendor driver notes reference similar issues.)
3) PCIe ASPM or power gating interacts with NVLink handshake causing link negotiation to fail and route DMA to invalid BARs. (Lower plausibility but matches correlation with BIOS power save settings.)
4) Kernel PCIe hotplug/IOMMU interactions: resume sequencing ordering bug causing device to be seen without required resources. (Medium plausibility.)

Data and observability we should add to the stack:
- Tag PM events in metrics pipeline (host-power-state transitions) and correlate with GPU error rates.
- Short term: add a resume-hook that emits structured event to tracing system with driver/firmware versions and PCIe link state.
- Capture early boot logs and persist dmesg across resume for affected hosts.

Longer-term remediation candidates:
- Upstream driver patch: ensure full DMA descriptor flush on suspend path and add sanity checks on resume. (Eng/Applied-ML + kernel driver team).
- Firmware microcode update coordination with GPU vendor; create vendor ticket with collected crash dumps and reproduction recipe.
- Fleet policy: default BIOS/UEFI power settings to disable aggressive ASPM in racks that run critical inference.

Open action items (owners):
- AVA: Assemble reproducible lab images and schedule 2-hour repro block with applied-ml (target: 2029-08-23).
- RAVI: Add resume-hook telemetry to cluster-agent that emits resume events to tracing (JIRA SRE-8472) (target: 2029-08-28).
- MAYA: Contact GPU vendor with Xid logs and crash dumps collected from lab (vendor ticket: TBD).
- LIAM: Draft fleet temporary policy to label hosts that underwent PM cycle in last 4h to avoid scheduling heavy inference (target: 2029-08-25).

Notes to self / oncall tips (informal):
- When you see a node that is "alive" but nvidia-smi returns "No devices found", resist the urge to modprobe/unload. Often the device is in partially enumerated state and forcing unload makes kernel oops worse. Prefer controlled reboot unless asked by lab team to experiment.
- Keep a copy of last-good kernel+driver combo for rollback; newer driver builds often change PM code paths.

Appendix: useful references and snippets:
- sample serverd resume hook (systemd): /etc/systemd/system/host-resume-notify.service -> ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/host-resume-notify --emit-event
- ipmi soft reboot: ipmitool -I lanplus -H <bmc> -U <user> -P <pass> chassis power soft
- kernel boot args quick try: add "pcie_aspm=off iommu=pt" to grub for test boot.

Current status: draft playbook — save notes here, tag relevant incidents, and iterate after first vendor response.

Document history: 2029-08-15 initial draft by Ava Martinez; 2029-08-18 added lab repro steps (Ravi); 2029-08-21 clarified mitigations and assigned owners.
